summary: The selected result group is a list of individual instances (rhombic dodecahedron, truncated octahedron, golden rhombohedra, cube-rhombic-dodecahedron intersections, a family of equal-edged space-filling zonohedra), each shown to be scissors congruent to a cube by explicit pieces. Each instance already follows from Debrunner's theorem for space-filling polyhedra or from Dehn-Sydler. Several are in the recreational dissection literature, and the submission itself claims no new mathematics, only the machine-checking. The input does not establish that this group of instances, as stated, would make a research paper or serious note, or name a research audience for these particular statements. The literature account is candid and mostly accurate. One part of the family definition (the 'nine most regular' space-fillers and the 'Bain rhombic dodecahedron') has neither a source nor a proof.

findings.message: Research interest is not shown. Each theorem in the group is a single instance of a classical fact. Every listed solid tiles space or has Dehn invariant zero, so Debrunner (1980) and Dehn-Sydler already give a scissors congruence to a cube, and several of the dissections are published recreational results (Frederickson; Hanegraaf; Theobald; Paterson). The submission says it claims no new dissections and no minimal piece counts; its only claim is that the dissections are machine-checked. Section 1 says formal correctness, the size of the Lean development and novelty do not by themselves establish research interest. The input names no research area or audience that would find these particular instance statements paper-worthy, and gives no reason why this list, rather than some other list, matters. A general statement would address this, for example: every parallelepiped, or every zonotope or parallelohedron, is scissors congruent to a cube of equal volume, proved once by a uniform construction; or a formal three-dimensional Wallace-Bolyai-Gerwien-type theorem for prisms. So would a stated audience, such as constructive scissors-congruence work or verified computational geometry, with evidence that the explicit pieces answer a question someone there has asked.

The family is partly defined by a claim that is neither sourced nor proved. The account says there are exactly 'nine most regular' space-fillers (equal-edged space-filling zonohedra with square, regular-hexagon and 60-degree-rhombus faces), and it names one of them the 'Bain rhombic dodecahedron'. No citation or argument supports the count of nine, and the name is not standard. The usual lists of space-filling zonohedra (for example, the Wikipedia tables of zonohedra and parallelohedra) have no such count and no such name. Either cite a classification, prove it, or present the solids simply as the listed explicit solids, without the completeness claim. Give each one its standard name or a description of how it is generated.

internal_notes.message: The input says Debrunner proved that every polyhedron that tiles space by congruent copies has Dehn invariant zero and is scissors congruent to a cube. Wikipedia states Debrunner's result for periodic tilings. The extension to arbitrary tilings is usually credited to Lagarias-Moews (1995), which the input cites as well. The Springer page could not be read, so this is not confirmed; the input should still check the wording. It is a minor attribution slip, not a finding: every listed solid tiles periodically, so nothing depends on it.

The input discloses that Debrunner was read through citations only, that Lagarias-Moews was read only as abstract and corollaries, and that Sah was not read. These are precise disclosures, not unsupported claims. The Frederickson/Theobald/Hanegraaf piece counts and the Paterson/Hanegraaf six-piece Demonstration match what search returned. The Debrunner citation details (Arch. Math. 35, 583-587) match, with a 1980/1981 date variance.

Independent search found no Lean, Isabelle, Coq, HOL or Mizar formalization of Sydler's theorem, the Wallace-Bolyai-Gerwien theorem or explicit three-dimensional dissections, which agrees with the input. Absence from a search does not prove novelty, and no priority is claimed.

Checked: in the cube ∩ rhombic dodecahedron solids the face-normal angles give dihedral angles of 90°, 120° and 135°. All are rational multiples of π, so the Dehn invariant is zero, as claimed. The golden rhombohedra are parallelepipeds, so they tile and have Dehn invariant zero.

The account puts the coordinates in ℚ(√2,√3,√5) adjoined the cube root of the volume. Going from the box to the cube by rectangle-to-rectangle steps (a×b to s×(ab/s)) stays inside the field generated by the box sides and s, which looks consistent. If the classical rectangle-to-square route is used instead, the square roots of products of box sides must be in the stated field; this should be checked when the proof is built.

Why notability falls just short: a verified, uniform, constructive scissors-congruence library (for example, any zonotope to a cube) would plausibly suit a CPP/ITP-style formalization paper and audience. Per-instance theorems over a hand-picked list do not show that by themselves. The proof is also not yet built.

what_would_reach_higher: Replace the per-instance list with a general theorem proved by one uniform construction: every parallelepiped is scissors congruent to a cube of equal volume (formal 3D Wallace-Bolyai-Gerwien-type step), then every zonotope (by its decomposition into parallelepipeds), or every parallelohedron. The listed solids then become corollaries.

Alternatively, prove a constructive theorem with a recognisable research audience, such as an explicit, effective version of Sydler's sufficiency for a defined class (for example, all polyhedra whose dihedral angles are rational multiples of π), and state it in the challenge.

Name the research audience and the question explicitly: who needs kernel-checked explicit pieces (constructive scissors congruence, verified computational geometry, certified dissection algorithms), with citations showing that the question has been asked.
Remove the 'nine most regular' completeness claim, or give a classification source or proof. Replace 'Bain rhombic dodecahedron' with a standard name or an explicit generator description.
Correct the Debrunner wording to periodic tilings and attribute the general (non-periodic) tiling result to Lagarias-Moews after reading it. Read Debrunner and Sah directly if possible.
Build the proof and a Comparator configuration, so that statement-level review and an exact declaration manifest are possible.
Cite related formal work on plane dissections or polygon equidecomposability, if any is found in the Lean/Isabelle/Coq ecosystems, to place the formal contribution.
